questions.stem: The record: A jury weighing a reasonableness standard claims the rule is too rigid. The legislature specified a numeric cutoff. Which account of the governing rule is faithful to the doctrine?

options.text: Rules offer predictability and constrain decision makers, while standards allow contextual judgment at the cost of greater uncertainty and discretion on this record.
A bright-line rule always produces better results because context should never matter in this instance.
Standards are always better because rigid rules cannot do justice in individual cases given the scenario.
Rules and standards are identical because both are simply instructions to a judge for this case.

questions.explanation: The choice is a institutional tradeoff. Rules reduce the room for bias and make outcomes predictable; standards let a decision maker respond to circumstances, but they shift power toward the decision maker. Here the decisive point is the tradeoff between rules and standards, so the result follows from that doctrine rather than from the surface appeal of a competing statement. Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.
questions.hint: Ask what each form gains and what it gives up. Keep the inquiry on the tradeoff between rules and standards.

questions.stem: This case: A jury weighing a reasonableness standard claims the rule is too rigid. The legislature specified a numeric cutoff. Which proposition would a court most likely rely on in resolving this dispute?

options.text: Discretion and arbitrariness are the same thing described in different words as applied here.
Discretion is structured judgment within legal limits, not a licence to choose any outcome the decision maker happens to prefer in the case at hand.
A judge with discretion may decide however she likes because no rule constrains her in the case at hand.
Any exercise of discretion is illegitimate because law should eliminate human judgment in the present case.

questions.explanation: Discretion operates inside a framework of relevant factors and reviewable reasons. A decision may be within discretion and still be wrong if it ignores a required consideration or relies on an improper one. Here the decisive point is the nature of judicial discretion, so the result follows from that doctrine rather than from the surface appeal of a competing statement. Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.
questions.hint: Ask which factors the decision maker was required to consider. Keep the inquiry on the nature of judicial discretion.

questions.stem: The dispute: A jury weighing a reasonableness standard claims the rule is too rigid. The legislature specified a numeric cutoff. Identify the statement that accurately reflects the applicable doctrine.

options.text: Any bright-line rule is irrational because real life has no sharp boundaries on the facts given.
A number in a rule guarantees that the result is substantively just in the circumstances.
A numeric cutoff gives clear guidance but necessarily creates hard cases just on either side of the line, where a small factual difference changes the result in this situation.
A precise threshold eliminates all borderline disputes on this record.
options.misconception: assumes a cutoff removes hard cases

questions.explanation: Thresholds buy clarity at the price of edge cases. The justification for a cutoff is administrative workability, so courts usually apply it even when a nearby case seems differently situated. Here the decisive point is bright-line thresholds and their limits, so the result follows from that doctrine rather than from the surface appeal of a competing statement. Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.
questions.hint: Ask what the line is buying in exchange for its harsh edges. Keep the inquiry on bright-line thresholds and their limits.
